https://www.dw.com/en/syria-says-deal-ag.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IWmG Assad's 2024 ouster was a blow to Russia's influence in the region [FILE: December 2024] Image: Leo Correa/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Syria and Russia have agreed on the future management of Russian bases on the country's Mediterranean coast. Russia used the bases to provide military support to former Syrian leader Bashar Assad during Syria's 13-year civil war that ended in 2024 . The Syrian Foreign Ministry announced Sunday that the two nations had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) after 18 months of negotiations . The deal effectively means Russia will no longer have military outposts in the Arab country. Syria says the strategic Mediterranean bases will become joint training centers [FILE: December 2024] Image: Adrien Vautier/Le Pictorium/IMAGO What will happen to Russia's military bases in Syria? Syria will take over management of the Hmeimim airport and the commercial berth at Tartus port, Syria's Foreign Ministry said. State media cited the ministry as saying that the bases would be converted into "joint training and capacity-building centres, within new arrangements that preserve mutual interests." The facilities will be gradually integrated into the country's civilian administration. The transition is expected to be completed within three months, the ministry said. Russia has yet to comment on the agreement. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani visited Tartus port on Sunday Image: SANA/AFP Russia trying to build relations with post-Assad Syria During the civil war in Syria between 2011 and 2024, while Assad was president, Russia was Syria's main ally and military backer. Assad was overthrown in December 2024 , and now lives in exile in Moscow. Current Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa led an alliance of Islamist rebel groups that fought against government forces during the war. Assad's ouster in 2024 dealt a major blow to Moscow's influence in the region. Russian President Vladimir Putin has been trying to build ties with Syria's new leadership to protect the future of the only two official Russian military bases located outside the former Soviet Union. Al-Sharaa has met with Putin in Moscow twice since coming to power in January 2025. During his last trip, Putin said, "much has been accomplished in terms of restoring our interstate relations." The Syrian government has been demanding that Moscow extradite Assad. Photograph: Mark Metcalfe/Getty Images Australia news Sydney Swans will sanction players for ‘serious breach’ over sexual assault allegations Club’s board meets on Tuesday night to decide penalties after league boss calls reports ‘deeply concerning’ Luca Ittimani and Jack Snape Tue 18 Aug 2026 07.18 EDT First published on Tue 18 Aug 2026 06.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Sydney Swans AFL club will decide on sanctions for players for “serious breach” of standards over an incident that led to a report of sexual assault. Victorian police on Tuesday confirmed the sexual crimes squad was investigating a reported sexual assault at Melbourne’s Pullman Hotel early on Monday morning. No arrests have been made and no charges have been laid. The Swans said the club had interviewed the players involved and its board would meet on Tuesday night to agree on penalties. “The club believes the players are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards, and it is appropriate to take firm action and highlight that any sanction we impose relates solely to those breaches,” the statement issued on Tuesday night said. The club did not name the players. The board’s decision is expected to be announced on Wednesday. The club said its actions would be independent of the ongoing police investigation and additional sanctions or decisions relating to police findings would wait until the investigation concluded. In the meantime, the club said it would “provide the appropriate support” to players, and their partners and families. The AFL’s chief executive, Andrew Dillon, said the league was ready to act on the “deeply concerning” allegations in a statement earlier on Tuesday evening. “Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met,” Dillon said. “Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light.” Dillon called for respect for the privacy of the woman who made the report to police. The Swans said they acknowledged the allegations impacted people other than the players, adding: “their wellbeing must be paramount”. “The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women,” the club said. AFLW athletes and staff were being offered support and their welfare was of “utmost importance,” the Swans said. The AFL has the power to stand down players if they are accused of illegal behaviour. No players have been stood down. Swans coach Dean Cox earlier on Tuesday said there would be updates “where we get more information,” when asked if there would be sanctions against any players. “We’re working our way through everything with the AFL and the relevant parties,” Cox said. Swans players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice were reportedly questioned by detectives in relation to the alleged incident. There is no confirmation they were directly involved. The four players reportedly returned to the hotel in the early hours of Monday morning after drinking, following the victory over Essendon at the MCG that secured the Swans a home final. The Swans play North Melbourne at the SCG on Sunday. Sydney is required to name its extended squad on Thursday evening then cut that back to 23 players plus three emergencies on Friday. The Swans then have a week off during the wildcard round before a home qualifying final. Dillon said the incident had wider ramifications for the AFL, beyond the impact on the Swans, in his Tuesday statement. “Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us,” he said. “Sexual assault allegations are serious, regardless of who is involved, what time of year it is, or what they may mean for a season.” Explore more on these topics Australia news AFL Sydney Swans Sydney New South Wales Australian rules football news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson was convicted over three deaths. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3vg.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, There have been concerns for security in the capital following the outbreak of fighting last week By Lucy Fleming ,Â BBC Africa Â and Â Teklemariam Bekit ,Â BBC Tigrinya Published 1 October 2026 Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say. The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region. A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes. "It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic. He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT). Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion. He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters. There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage. The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment. Meanwhile, Ethiopia's foreign ministry has said it is closing its embassy in neighbouring Eritrea and expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats "for involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security". Earlier, in a BBC interview, Eritrea's government denied that it was backing the new rebel alliance. Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? Published 6 days ago WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? Published 3 days ago Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). They both accuse each other of violating a 2022 peace deal that ended a brutal two-year civil war, which according to an Africa Union mediator is estimated to have cost 600,000 lives. Last month, seven armed movements, including the TPLF and an Amhara militia known as Fano, formed an alliance with the stated aim of removing the government in Addis Ababa. There is disagreement over which side started the latest fighting. The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. It is difficult to verify what is happening on the ground and access to the internet and the main telecoms service provider in Tigray have also been cut. Within Tigray, the national army and a pro-government militia appear to be advancing towards the region's main city of Mekelle. In the southern Tigrayan town of Alamata, a medic told the BBC on Wednesday that 52 civilians had died in three days of heavy fighting . The TPLF is also reported to be fighting in neighbouring Afar region, a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports. A humanitarian source has estimated that tens of thousands have fled their homes in Afar, according to the AFP news agency. Fighting around Lalibela in the Amhara region, a Unesco world heritage site where foreign tourists have been stranded for more than a week, has involved the national army and Fano fighters, now allied to the TPLF. The government has accused neighbouring Eritrea of backing these groups. One pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers were involved on the front lines. But in a rare response to the BBC from Eritrea's government, Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel dismissed the allegations. He accused Ethiopia's ruling Prosperity Party (PP) of seeking external scapegoats for the country's mounting challenges. "The PP regime has made it a habit to apportion blame to its neighbours in order to deflect attention from the myriad internal conflicts that it is fomenting in various parts of the country," he told BBC Tigrinya. Eritrea was a key ally of Ethiopia during the Tigray war, fighting against the TPLF. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports. Ethiopia lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Abiy has even hinted at taking the port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - by force as he sees direct access to the sea as important for Ethiopia's long-term future and economic prosperity. As concerns over security mount in Ethiopia, the country's National Intelligence and Security Service (Niss) announced on Wednesday that it was imposing an indefinite ban on drone flights in Addis Ababa and surrounding areas. The agency said it would not issue permits for drone operations and warned that legal action would be taken against anyone flying drones in restricted areas. Niss said the measure was necessary to protect national leaders, critical infrastructure and major public events. Photograph: Don Arnold/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The locations of Jewish gatherings across Australia’s capital cities have not been publicised as community members report ongoing fears for their safety. Photograph: Don Arnold/Getty Images Australia news Australian leaders condemn pro-Palestine vigils planned for 7 October anniversary amid Jewish commemorations Peak Jewish bodies organise ceremonies on third anniversary of attacks that triggered conflict in which 74,000 Palestinians have been killed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Mon 5 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 10.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jewish Australians will mark the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks on Wednesday as Labor state governments condemn pro-Palestinian vigils to be held the same day. Peak Jewish bodies have organised commemorations across the capital cities but avoided publicising locations as community members report ongoing fears for their safety since the Bondi terror attack in December. Hamas militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage in the surprise attack on Israel in 2023, triggering the ongoing Israel-Gaza war in which 74,000 Palestinians have been killed . On the night before the anniversary, people at a Melbourne event were expected to hear a first-hand account from an Israeli soldier who was in the country during the attacks. Zionism Victoria has planned an outdoor evening ceremony on Wednesday. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Sydney’s eastern suburbs will host a dawn commemoration starting at 6.29am, to mark the time at which Hamas’ attack began and an evening community event run by the Zionist Council of NSW and backed by the United Israel Appeal, the local arm of Keren Hayesod. “United in remembrance and resilience, we stand with Israel and the Jewish people, joined by our fellow Australians against hatred and extremism,” the evening event’s description reads. A documentary exploring experiences of Israeli trauma professionals, After Never Again, will be screened in Canberra and Perth. The film has been produced by Kehilot to Australia or K2A, a group set up to bring Israeli youth to Australia for relief from the stress of living near active conflict. View image in fullscreen The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has said the planned vigils on the anniversary of a ‘horrible and violent event were ‘obscene’. Photograph: George Chan/Getty Images All details, including registration, have been kept private for events planned in Brisbane and Adelaide. JWire has reported the Zionist Council of Queensland has organised a gathering open to Nepalese, Filipino and Iranian communities. Pro-Palestine groups have also planned to mark the day, with a gathering planned at Sydney’s town hall on Wednesday evening. An organising group, Jews Against The Occupation ‘48, said their event would not be a protest but a vigil to mark Israel’s retaliatory airstrikes on Gaza on 7 October 2023, in a post on social media. Wollongong Friends of Palestine, south of Sydney, has planned its own vigil. A Melbourne “sit-in vigil” is planned from 10am to 5pm outside the state library of Victoria. The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll , has said police would act to “protect the public” if the event breached the state’s anti-vilification laws. ‘I didn’t go looking for trouble’: Protester sues NSW after allegedly being punched by police at Herzog rally Read more The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns , has said the planned vigils on the anniversary of a “horrible and violent” event were “obscene”, speaking to reporters last Wednesday. “To choose that day, I think it’s designed to antagonise large sections of our community,” Minns said. “I’m obviously distressed on their behalf.” Minns said supreme court and high court decisions on political communication prevented him from shutting down the Wednesday gatherings. “They’re very difficult … for us to shut down static protests, particularly ones, as I think they’re describing it as a vigil, a silent vigil. We’ll see if it is a silent vigil.” Further pro-Palestine rallies to mark the anniversary are planned in more than a dozen Australian cities on Sunday as part of a “global day of action” led by activist groups overseas. A Friday rally is also scheduled outside the electorate office of Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles. https://www.politico.eu/article/romania-.text: Romanian President Nicușor Dan faces demands from allies and adversaries alike to call a snap election, the first in the country’s modern history, if his latest attempt to end five months of political paralysis fails. The key NATO and EU member has lacked a fully functioning government since the coalition collapsed in May, and lawmakers have rejected a succession of Dan’s prime ministerial nominees. Political parties are now weighing up whether to support Dan’s latest prime ministerial candidate, the diplomat Luca Niculescu, who must win a confidence vote in parliament within the next nine days to be confirmed in the role. Advertisement Advertisement In an interview, Dan’s arch-rival on Romania’s hard right, George Simion, warned that no stable government can form without an election and accused the president of mounting a “blockade” against democracy because he is “afraid of us coming to power.” Speaking separately to POLITICO, Dan’s most recently defeated candidate for prime minister, Member of the European Parliament Siegfried Mureșan, warned the country was already paying an economic price, with investment decisions being delayed. “Postponing early elections and staying in this stalemate situation would, at some point, also have economic negative consequences,” he said. Bordering Ukraine, Romania has the sixth-largest population in the EU and plays a critical role in NATO’s defense of the region as home to a major military base and a U.S. missile shield site. The country has been plagued by political instability, corruption and a ballooning budget deficit in recent years, conditions that have fueled a surge in support for hard-right nationalist politics. Since the coalition fell apart amid infighting over budget cuts in the spring, Romania’s deadlocked parliament has been unable to agree on a new government. Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) leader Simion, a staunch euroskeptic who has called for a halt to aid for Ukraine, told POLITICO the president must face his duty and give voters a chance to end the stalemate with a fresh election, or face being ousted. His party has been leading Romania’s opinion polls for almost two years. Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president, which he believes will gain momentum if Niculescu fails and Dan again refuses to call fresh elections. Advertisement Advertisement “Everybody says, ‘OK, if this won’t pass, we will go to snap elections,’ but they do not know Nicușor Dan as I do,” Simion said. The president is “very stubborn” and could defy calls for elections even if all parties want them, he said. “In that case we will have the numbers of signatures and votes to suspend him at least, if not sack him.” Dan has refused to contemplate handing AUR a role in government. He defeated Simion for the presidency last year and regards his rival’s politics as a threat to Romania’s pro-Western, pro-European direction . The president says he opposes a snap election because the campaign period would delay budget reforms and healthcare funding. ‘A new Greece’ The Romanian leu has weakened against the euro in the months since the crisis blew up. Simion urged international investors to remain patient and sought to reassure them that AUR would be fiscally responsible if it won power. “Nobody wants a new Greece,” he said. “We will do everything it takes to respect our commitments to our international partners and for them to recover the debts.” The call for an early election is gaining traction in Bucharest. So far, the leader of Dan’s former party, the Save Romania Union, has joined politicians from the National Liberal Party, and the leader of the Social Democratic Party and AUR, in suggesting an unprecedented emergency election could be required. George Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president. | Robert Ghement/EPA Dan’s latest plan still has time to work, but political feuding between parties remains a problem. The Liberals say they could support Niculescu as prime minister if the Social Democrats do not get too much influence, while the Social Democrats say they want the PM-designate to take the country in a new direction — away from the austerity policies of the outgoing Liberal premier, Ilie Bolojan. Advertisement Advertisement Mureșan, a pro-EU Liberal and European People’s Party vice-president, said the economic risks of prolonging the crisis were real. He told POLITICO a snap election could be inevitable, though this is not his “preferred” option. “The political uncertainty which exists now in the country can easily transform into economic uncertainty,” Mureșan warned. “We are already now seeing investors holding back on their investments, waiting with major investment decisions before they have more certainty.” While Mureșan said he wants Dan to succeed, he criticized the delays in resolving the longest-running crisis since the fall of communism in 1989. “Had the president moved fast in appointing a prime minister in May and not delayed the nominations, we might even have had early elections [by] now, and we would be in a situation with a new parliament, and with a stable government with the four-year agenda,” he said. “So, clearly, the options are narrowing down and are not getting better, following the prolongation of the political crisis.”
